newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss acknowledge confidential 1949 Polish deal.
newsitem.headline: Swiss acknowledge confidential 1949 Polish deal.

text.p: Switzerland acknowledged on Friday that it had done a confidential deal with Poland in 1949 to liquidate Polish citizens' unclaimed wealth, but denied charges that this had let it keep property of Jewish Holocaust victims.

The arrangement was detailed in an exchange of letters dated June 25, 1949, but not published at the time, the Swiss foreign ministry said in a statement. Under it, unclaimed Polish funds in Switzerland were to be turned over to Poland's central bank.

The letters were in conjunction with a previously publicised agreement that provided for Poland to pay Switzerland 52.1 million Swiss francs ($41 million at 1996 rates) in compensation for property the then-communist Polish regime had nationalised.

"Various sides alleged yesterday that Switzerland struck a secret accord with Poland after World War Two that let Switzerland seize for itself dormant assets of Polish citizens," the ministry statement said. "This allegation is wrong."
Switzerland also struck post-war compensation accords with Bulgaria, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, Romania and Hungary, it said.

The ministry said it was trying to clear up other open questions on post-war agreements, especially whether the assets were actually handed over to the governments with whom the arrangements were made, when and how much was involved.

Switzerland on Thursday denied a U.S. senator's assertion that Berne had struck secret deals that let it tap the unclaimed wealth of Eastern European Jews to compensate Swiss citizens for property nationalised by communist regimes.

Senator Alfonse D'Amato, whose Senate Banking Committee is probing the fate of Jewish wealth left in Swiss banks by Holocaust victims, said researchers had found documents showing the Swiss struck just such a secret deal in 1949 with Poland and subsequently with Hungary and Czechoslovakia.
